archetype.name: Pocket Passer (vertical)
archetype.definition: A strong-armed thrower who stays in the pocket, rarely runs, and earns his value pushing the ball down the field from clean platforms in a run-first offense.

report.headline: Big-play arm, cleaner throws, but the middle of the field still bites him
report.take:
Penix took the job in Week 3, after Cooper Rush and Tua Tagovailoa each started a game, and he has played the way his first two seasons suggested. He is a pocket passer in an offense that does not want to throw. Atlanta's pass rate over expected is -8.3, 29th in the league, and he is not a runner either: 15 rushing yards, five scrambles in 184 dropbacks. His value comes from the arm. On throws of 20+ air yards he is at +1.031 EPA per play, and his 10+ yard throws are at +0.403. Everything under 10 yards nets out slightly negative, because 36 throws behind the line cost 19 points of EPA. His season grade is roughly average (+0.018 EPA per dropback, 25th of 47). That average is a good vertical passer weighed down by a screen game that is not working.

The biggest real change is how clean the throws are. His bad-throw rate was 21.9% as a rookie and 22.5% last year, ranking 58th and 59th in those seasons. It is 11.3% now, eighth of 38. He is getting the ball out 0.21 seconds faster than last year, and he is throwing from the cleanest pocket in the league: pressured on 11.9% of dropbacks, the lowest rate among qualifiers, behind a line whose hit rate allowed ranks second. Completion percentage over expected (CPOE) is still poor at -4.59, but that has been true every year of his career, so it is part of who he is. The split shows where it comes from: +3.1 on short throws and +3.1 deep, -8.9 on intermediate throws and -18.7 behind the line.

The numbers hide two things. First, his positive EPA leans on two early blowouts. When leading by 9+ he is at +1.085 a play on 20 plays. In one-score games he is at -0.115 across 103 plays, and trailing by 9+ he is at -0.120. Second, the middle of the field is a problem. Throws there are at -0.285 EPA, with three of his five interceptions on only 28 attempts. To the left he has six touchdowns, no picks and +0.279 a play. He reads and throws outside well. He has not yet shown he can work the hashes against coverage that sits there.

The last three games look awful (-0.257 EPA per dropback, -11 CPOE), and most of that is one afternoon. At Tampa, against the league's second-ranked defense, he went 8 of 24 with four interceptions and -24.1 EPA. In the two games before it he threw six touchdowns. The trend is volatile rather than collapsing. His interceptions per game have already caught up to his touchdown rate, though, and that bears watching against any defense that can take away the outside.

strengths.title: Wins the deep shot
strengths.body: His 16 throws of 20+ air yards have produced +1.031 EPA per play with a positive CPOE. Big gains on a small sample are fragile, but his yards per attempt ranked inside the top 22 in both prior seasons too, so the vertical arm is real. It is the reason he is efficient despite a below-average completion rate.

strengths.title: Far fewer wild throws
strengths.body: His bad-throw rate has dropped 11.2 points from last year, from near the bottom of the league to eighth. A quicker release and the league's cleanest pocket explain much of it. Because it is such a sharp break from his career, expect some of it to give back if the pressure rises.

strengths.title: Two efficient primary targets
strengths.body: Drake London (52 targets, +0.432 EPA per target) and Kyle Pitts (+0.401) are where his value lands, and the passing game runs left through them. That is a stable base. Neither is on the injury report.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: He is rarely pressured, but when he is, 42.9% of those pressures end in sacks, the worst rate among 38 qualifiers. That is not the cost of extending plays, since he barely scrambles. It is a pocket passer holding the ball. A line this good hides it, and a defense that wins quickly will expose it.

concerns.title: Middle-of-field turnovers
concerns.body: Over the middle his CPOE is -13.6 and his EPA is negative, with three interceptions in 28 attempts. His interception rate is 3.0%, 36th of 47, after he threw just three picks in each of his first two seasons. Part of this is one bad day at Tampa. The middle-of-field misses are a pattern that needs to change.

concerns.title: Efficiency lives in blowouts
concerns.body: Nearly all of his positive EPA came while leading by 9+. In one-score games he is below average. Some of that is the early GB and NO routs, but it means his true level in competitive games is lower than the season line.

trend.note: He was efficient in each of his first three starts, posted negative EPA in a three-touchdown loss to Chicago, was sharp against San Francisco, then had a four-interception shutout at Tampa. The swings track the opponent and game script more than a steady slide.

nextGame.headline: Shootout script and soft underneath coverage, but Cincinnati gets home
nextGame.body:
Cincinnati sets up well for volume. Its offense ranks fifth in EPA and fourth passing, and it passes 8 points over expected, the most in the league. The 52.5 total is the highest of any game he has started, and the Falcons are home underdogs at +136. That should pull a run-first offense into more dropbacks than usual. Through the air, the Bengals' defense is middling (13th in pass EPA) and soft underneath (27th on short throws), and quarterbacks have averaged 289 yards a game against them, 30th. Two things cut the other way. They are stingy deep (sixth), which is his best area, and their sack rate is second in the league, which goes straight at his worst habit.

Availability mostly helps him. Corner DJ Turner II, a 95%-snap starter, is questionable with an ankle injury and listed day-to-day. If he sits, the outside throws to London get easier. Safety Kyle Dugger is out, but he plays only a part-time role. On Atlanta's side, Zachariah Branch (hamstring) and backup back Brian Robinson Jr. are out. Neither changes much, since Branch has been a negative-EPA, part-time target. The line and both primary receivers are intact.

keyMatchups.title: Penix's hold against Cincinnati's rush
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati sacks quarterbacks at the second-highest rate, and he converts pressure into sacks more often than any qualifier. If the Bengals win early downs, drive-killing sacks are the likeliest way this game goes wrong. The quicker release he has shown this year is the counter.

keyMatchups.title: Pitts against a leaky TE defense
keyMatchups.body: Top tight ends have scored 3.9 PPR over their averages against Cincinnati, 30th of 32. Tight ends also draw a larger share of targets against the Bengals than the league norm. That is a natural outlet for Pitts, and it suits a defense that gives up the short game.

keyMatchups.title: Game script and pass volume
keyMatchups.body: Atlanta's run-first lean caps his volume, and its 29th-ranked pass rate over expected says so. A Bengals offense this efficient and pass-happy may force Atlanta's hand. More dropbacks raise both his yardage ceiling and his interception exposure.

nextGame.watch: Whether he gets the ball out against Cincinnati's pass rush instead of taking sacks, and whether he avoids forcing throws into the middle of the field.

restOfSeason.body:
The base is real. He has a clean pocket, a dependable outside game to London and Pitts, and a deep ball that has carried his efficiency across three seasons. Expect yardage in the 195 to 250 range most weeks, limited by a run-first plan more than by his arm. The red-zone line (seven touchdowns, no picks, despite a 41.9% completion rate) is likely to cool. So is the near-perfect deep efficiency on 16 throws, which leaves touchdowns around 1.2 to 1.8 a game.

The interception rate should settle back toward his career norm, since one game produced most of it. But the middle-of-field problems and the worst pressure-to-sack rate in the league mean good pass defenses will keep producing duds. The bad-throw gains will probably give back some ground. His CPOE is likely to stay below average, as it has every year. Taken together, he projects as a roughly league-average starter with big weeks in shootouts and a floor that can drop out.
swingFactors: How often game script forces Atlanta to throw
Whether the clean pocket holds up

confidence.note: Only six starts, with one extreme game skewing the recent numbers, but his core traits match his first two seasons.
